author: AfricanFeminism
title: Morocco’s First Woman Prime Minister and the Terms of Freedom
content:
Something changes when a woman occupies an office men have treated as their natural inheritance. Fatima Ezzahra El Mansouri’s 

appointment

 on 29 September 2026 makes that change visible in Morocco. For women whose competence is routinely scrutinised, the pleasure is neither naïve nor trivial.




But the woman forming a government and the woman labouring in the fields, raising children without pay and denied an equal share of her inheritance encounter power differently. Representation changes who governs; emancipation changes what all women have the power to do. That distinction shifts our attention from PM Mansouri’s gender to the politics of the centre-right

 Party of Authenticity and Modernity (PAM

)

, which she leads. Will its programme redistribute the resources and rights on which women’s freedom depends?




The history beneath the headline




Calling women’s leadership foreign to Morocco requires forgetting its history. Historian Osire Glacier 

documents

 women’s authority long before the contemporary premiership. Kenza al Awrabiya, the Amazigh mother of Idris II, helped secure the Idrisid dynasty, founded in the late eighth century in what is now Morocco. Zaynab al Nafzawiyya influenced eleventh-century Almoravid politics around Aghmat, near Marrakech. Sayyida al Hurra governed Tétouan, a city in northern Morocco, during the sixteenth century. author: AfricanFeminism
title: Feminist Spaces: Abusive Power and the Accountability We Owe
content:
Feminist spaces are not toxic. Feminism is not toxic. Accountability is not toxic.




So, what is?




This began as my rage, but now it is my love letter to the movement.




A call to do better. To be better. To build spaces worthy of the feminism we claim.




This piece is born from my rage. From the nights I spent questioning whether I was too sensitive, too difficult, too much. From the moments I swallowed my truth because speaking it would cost me opportunities, contracts, references, relationships, or my place in the movement. From the realization that I was being asked to trade my voice for access, my dignity for opportunity, my growth for loyalty and the truth is… I am done trading.




I know I am not alone. This is not just my story. It is the story of countless women, feminists, workers, and young people who have been asked to choose between their voice and their livelihood, between their dignity and their place in the room.




Maybe you know this feeling. The tightness in your chest before a meeting. The way you edit yourself mid-sentence. The calculations you make: 

If I say this, will I lose that contract? That reference? That place at the table?

author: AfricanFeminism
title: Naming the Violence: FGM Survivors Take Their Fight for Justice Online
content:
I was just 17 years old, in a WhatsApp group with peers discussing sexual and gender-based violence when I first heard that Female Genital Mutilation (FGM) was violence. I remember being agitated by the turn the discussion took. Though much of that conversation is murky now, I remember repeating the same lines: ‘

FGM is culture; if we can advocate for abortion, then surely we could allow others to practise their culture in peace

’. A colleague then insinuated that such statements were why more girls and women were being harmed – that I was, in fact, supporting violence against women and girls.




Teenage me had just started her activism journey, but carried the authority of someone who thought she knew it all. For her, FGM was a normal part of existence. My mother, aunties, cousins and almost every woman I knew had gone through it. I had heard stories of older women travelling for days to be cut. Being cut was an honour. Families paid the woman who performed the cutting. There was no way, teenage me would think, that love and violence could coexist. So being called a perpetrator on that platform did not sit well with her.




I left pressed to prove someone wrong. I decided to learn more about FGM, hoping to win the next argument. I dove into its history, beyond what I had absorbed socially.

author: AfricanFeminism
title: Who Can Afford to Imagine Liberation?
content:
I recently had a conversation with an acquaintance who had applied for activist welfare support after the floods in Accra, Ghana this June destroyed much of what they owned. Their appliances, gadgets and other belongings were gone or damaged, rent was still due, and they had the very reasonable fear that the rains could return and the next flood could be worse. They work full-time with a grassroots organization, which can mean having a job without necessarily having the financial security to suddenly move house, replace their belongings and start again. They never received feedback on that application. Through the kind of backdoor follow-up that has become an unofficial administrative system of its own in social justice movements, they eventually learned that the welfare fund was specifically for activists who needed relocation, medical assistance, provisions and other forms of support as a result of their activism.




I understand why such a fund exists. People face threats, violence and displacement because of the politics of the work, and there should be resources when that happens. But I kept returning to the question of what counts as care in activism and what has to happen before suffering becomes recognizable as an activist emergency. A flooded home is an emergency. author: AfricanFeminism
title: Beyond Translation: Reimagining Feminist Funding for Portuguese-Speaking Africa
content:
“Portuguese-speaking Africa is not on the margins of Africa’s feminist movement. It is an essential part of it.”




Across Africa, feminist movements have long challenged systems of inequality, responded to crises, created new possibilities for minoritized and excluded communities. Philanthropy has been integral to advances toward just and equal African societies. Yet within the current global and continental landscape of feminist philanthropy, some communities and movements remain largely unseen. 




The Portuguese-speaking African countries that include Angola, Cabo Verde, Guinea-Bissau, Mozambique, Equatorial Guinea and São Tomé and Principe, represent diverse histories, political realities and social contexts. Their feminist movements are dynamic, innovative and deeply rooted in their communities. They are advancing gender justice in contexts shaped by economic deprivation and inequality, climate change, difficult democratic transitions, shrinking civic space and gender-based violence.




Despite this important work, these movements continue to face significant barriers to accessing resources, networks and spaces where Africa’s feminist priorities are shaped. The challenge is not a lack of organizing. It is a fragmented funding ecosystem that has not yet fully recognized or responded to the diversity of Africa’s feminist movements.

author: AfricanFeminism
title: Para além da tradução: repensar o financiamento feminista na África lusófona
content:
“A África lusófona não está à margem do movimento feminista africano. É uma parte integrante dele.”




Em toda a África, os movimentos feministas há muito que desafiam os sistemas de desigualdade, respondem às crises e criam novas possibilidades para as comunidades marginalizadas e excluídas. A filantropia tem sido fundamental para os avanços rumo a sociedades africanas justas e igualitárias. No entanto, no atual panorama global e continental da filantropia feminista, algumas comunidades e movimentos continuam, em grande parte, invisíveis. 




Os países africanos de língua portuguesa entre os quais se incluem Angola, Cabo Verde, Guiné-Bissau, Moçambique, Guiné Equatorial e São Tomé e Príncipe representam histórias, realidades políticas e contextos sociais diversos. Os seus movimentos feministas são dinâmicos, inovadores e profundamente enraizados nas suas comunidades. Estão a promover a justiça de género em contextos marcados pela privação económica e pela desigualdade, pelas alterações climáticas, por transições democráticas difíceis, pela redução do espaço cívico e pela violência baseada no género.




Apesar deste importante trabalho, estes movimentos continuam a enfrentar obstáculos significativos no acesso a recursos, redes e espaços onde se definem as prioridades feministas de África. O desafio não reside na falta de organização. Trata-se de um ecossistema de financiame

author: Rosebell Kagumire
title: Who Does “Mutual Interest” Serve in an Unequal World? On EU Development Cooperation Pivot
content:
What is mutual interest in an unequal world? That’s what I was reflecting on this week in Brussels, when I joined the “Mutual interests in practice: How should Global Europe balance development, economic and geopolitical objectives?” panel at The Future of EU Development Cooperation, hosted by the European Centre for Development Policy Management (ECDPM) and Oxfam. The discussion came at a decisive moment, as the EU negotiates its next long-term budget and the Global Europe Instrument, while the Commission prepares for consultations with civil society and local authorities from 28 September to 1 October. Regional sessions include “Sub-Saharan Africa”, while global thematic sessions cover human development, the green and digital transition, democracy and human rights, and partnerships.

The EU is pivoting development cooperation towards its own economic, security and foreign policy goals through a “mutual interest” approach. But mutual interest means little unless it confronts the unequal systems that determine whose interests count, whose risks are ignored, and whose lives are rendered negotiable.
